notes:
# Hosea 8 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter
The chapter forms part of "the prophecy of judgment" (Hosea 8:1–10:15). It catalogs Israel's sins — covenant-breaking, hypocritical worship, self-appointed kings, the golden calves, foreign alliances, multiplying altars, rejecting God's law, and forgetting their Maker — each paired with a corresponding judgment. The central metaphor is v. 7: sowing the wind, reaping the whirlwind.

*Sources: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary); Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

---

## v. 1 — "Put the ram’s horn to your lips! An eagle looms over the house of the LORD…"

**The trumpet (shophar/ram's horn):** A command to sound the alarm of imminent invasion. The shophar was used to warn of danger (Ezek 33:3–6; Jer 4:5–6), to summon troops (Num 10:1–10), or to announce holy assemblies (Lev 23:24). Here it signals that judgment is at the door. Even this warning is an act of mercy — God gives one final opportunity to repent before the eagle descends.

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary)*

**The "eagle" (or vulture):** The Hebrew *nesher* may refer to a griffon vulture. The invading Assyrian army is pictured as a bird of prey swooping swiftly and irresistibly. The image emphasizes speed, power, and inevitability. This fulfills Moses' covenant curse in Deut 28:49: "The LORD will bring a nation against you from afar… as the eagle swoops down."

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary); NET Bible notes (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

**"House of the LORD":** Ellicott says Hosea uses this phrase "with some irony" — it refers to the Northern Kingdom (Samaria), not the Jerusalem temple. Though the calf at Bethel was meant to symbolize Israel's God, Hosea gives the nation the name "House of Jehovah" to highlight the tragedy: God's own covenant people have become the target of His judgment. Gill understands it as "the nation of Israel, formerly called the house and family of God, and still pretended to be so."

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

**"Transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law":** Two charges. To *transgress* (*ʿābar*) means to cross a boundary — Israel deliberately stepped over the limits of the Mosaic covenant. To *rebel* (*pasha*) is stronger: it denotes willful, high-handed rejection of rightful authority, like a wife abandoning her husband or a subject raising the banner of revolt against his king. The Mosaic covenant is viewed as a marriage covenant, making Israel's idolatry spiritual adultery.

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary)*

**Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic):** The trumpet summons the Assyrians as God's instrument of judgment, not merely announcing judgment in the abstract.

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

---

## v. 2 — "Israel cries out to Me, 'O our God, we know You!'"

**Insincere profession:** In the face of calamity, Israel loudly claims covenant relationship: "My God, we know You!" But the cry is hollow. They wanted God's protection without God's rule, His blessings without obedience. Their words reveal religious presumption, not genuine devotion.

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary)*

**Guzik** connects this to Jesus' warning in Matthew 7:22–23: "Many will say to Me in that day, 'Lord, Lord' … And then I will declare to them, 'I never knew you; depart from Me.'"

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**Ellicott** renders it: "To me they cry, My God, we know Thee, we Israel" — the addition of "we Israel" underscoring their appeal to national election while their lives denied it.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**Gill** notes the cry is "in a hypocritical manner" — they own God as the true God and claim interest in Him, though they have worshipped idols for hundreds of years. He cites Titus 1:16: "They profess to know God, but in works they deny Him."

*Source: Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

---

## v. 3 — "But Israel has rejected good; an enemy will pursue him."

**"Rejected good":** The "good" (*tov*) likely refers to God Himself — the chief Good. Aben Ezra (cited by Ellicott) says it is "the name of God, which is the salvation of Israel." The word translated "cast off" or "rejected" (*zanach*) carries a sense of scornful loathing — treating with disgust something that ought to be precious.

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

**"Enemy will pursue him":** The eagle of v. 1 — Assyria under Shalmaneser — will chase Israel down. No escape is possible once God's protection is forfeited.

---

## v. 4 — "They set up kings, but not by Me…"

**Self-appointed kings:** A reference to the political anarchy of the Northern Kingdom after Jeroboam II's death. Conspirators like Shallum, Menahem, Pekah, and Hoshea seized the throne through assassination and without seeking God's direction. Though Jeroboam I's revolt had received divine sanction (1 Kings 11:9–11), the later pattern of usurpation and murder was wholly without God's approval.

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

**Guzik** quotes Boice: "To choose leaders without the direction of God is not only sinful, it is foolish. Those who follow their own wisdom in the choice of leaders inevitably get what they deserve."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**NET Bible note:** The phrase "but without My approval" translates "but without me" — literally "I did not know" (i.e., did not recognize or acknowledge).

*Source: NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

**"With their silver and gold they made themselves idols, to their own destruction":** The NET note says the phrase "that they might be cut off" is ironic — they made idols for prosperity, but the result was the opposite: their own destruction. The silver and gold could not save them.

*Source: NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

---

## v. 5 — "He has rejected your calf, O Samaria…"

**The calf of Samaria:** The golden calf-idol originally set up by Jeroboam I at Bethel (and Dan) to prevent the Northern tribes from worshipping at Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26–33). It was meant to represent Yahweh, but God utterly rejected this man-made worship as idolatry.

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary)*

**"He has rejected" — or "your calf stinks":** Guzik notes the Hebrew is literally "your calf stinks" (citing Wood). Ellicott renders "is loathsome" and says "Nothing can exceed the scorn of this outburst."

*Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**"How long will they be incapable of innocence?":** NET renders this as "They will not survive much longer without being punished." Ellicott: "How long are ye unable to attain purity?" The question implies that after all the warnings and judgments, Israel remains stubbornly impure — incapable of cleansing themselves from idolatry.

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

---

## v. 6 — "For this thing is from Israel — a craftsman made it, and it is not God…"

**Man-made, therefore not God:** A devastatingly simple argument. If a human artisan fashioned it, it cannot be deity. The calf originated "from Israel" — it was their own invention, not divine revelation. Gill says this is "a strong and invincible reason … a creature cannot make a God, or give that which itself has not."

*Sources: Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**"Broken to pieces":** Ellicott translates "shattered to fragments" or "become splinters or fine dust." This may allude to Moses grinding the golden calf to powder (Exodus 32:20).

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

---

## v. 7 — "For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind…"

**The central proverb of the chapter:** "Wind" represents the emptiness and futility of idolatry and political scheming. "Whirlwind" represents the far greater devastation of divine judgment. The principle is that the harvest always corresponds to the sowing, but is far greater in magnitude. Sin compounded over time reaps a concentrated, overwhelming judgment (cf. Gal 6:7–8).

*Sources: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**Ellicott** adds a spiritual dimension: the punishment for sin is often a greater facility in sinning — indifference to God becomes enmity; forgetfulness of duty becomes violent recoil from truth.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**Guzik** notes: "It will seem to Israel that the judgment they receive is worse than the sin they committed. This isn't true in the sense of God being worse to us than our sin deserves, but it is true in how judgment feels … our sin is sown over a long period of time, but often reaped in a contracted period of judgment."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**The agricultural imagery:** "No standing grain … fails to yield flour … foreigners would swallow it." Even if the crop shows promise, it produces nothing usable — and if it does, invaders consume it anyway. All of Israel's efforts at prosperity through idolatry and alliances would come to nothing.

**Spurgeon preached a sermon on this verse titled "What Will the Harvest Be?"** (noted at Precept Austin). The full sermon text was not retrievable, but the title emphasizes the inevitable link between sowing and reaping.

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_hosea)*

---

## v. 8 — "Israel is swallowed up! Now they are among the nations like a worthless vessel."

**"Swallowed up":** Not just their land's produce, but the nation itself — consumed and destroyed by Assyria as if devoured by a wild beast. The present tense is used prophetically for the certainty of the future event.

*Source: Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

**"Worthless vessel" (vessel wherein is no pleasure):** A piece of pottery broken, useless, fit only for the vilest purposes — or smashed as worthless. Gill says they were treated "with the utmost neglect and contempt … no more regarded than a vessel of dishonour, that is made and used for the ease of nature." Ellicott compares Jer 48:38, Ps 31:13, and 2 Tim 2:20.

*Sources: Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**NET Bible:** "They will be like a worthless piece of pottery."

*Source: NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

---

## v. 9 — "For they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own. Ephraim has hired lovers."

**"Gone up to Assyria":** Ellicott notes the irony — the verb "go up" is normally used for "going up" to the sanctuary of the Lord. Instead, Israel goes up to Assyria for help.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**"Wild donkey alone by itself":** The wild ass (*pered*) of the steppes is an image of untamed waywardness, stubborn independence, and lustful wandering. Normally these animals travel in herds, but here Israel is pictured as a solitary donkey, alone and vulnerable — having isolated herself from God, she is easy prey for the Assyrian lion. Ellicott notes that from Jer 2:24 we infer the animal wanders alone after the object of its lust, and Israel, "like a solitary wild ass, seeks strange loves, courts strange alliances."

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm); Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/hosea-8.html)*

**"Ephraim has hired lovers":** By paying tribute to Assyria and Egypt (2 Kings 15:19), Israel "hired" foreign powers as political allies. But the language is deliberately sexual — "lovers" — framing political alliances as spiritual adultery against Yahweh, Israel's true Husband (cf. Ezek 16:32–34). Ellicott notes: "Ephraim pays abnormally for her own shame."

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

---

## v. 10 — "Though they hire allies among the nations, I will now round them up…"

**Interpretation debated.** Ellicott outlines two main views:
1. **"I will gather them (Israel) together"** — God will round Israel up in restraint so they can no longer roam wildly seeking help, and they will sorrow under the tribute burden of "the king of princes" (the Assyrian monarch). This accords with Hos 2:8–9 and 3:4. The non-payment of tribute actually occurred a few years later (2 Kings 17:4, when Hoshea withheld tribute).
2. **"I will gather these nations"** — God assembles the nations to look scornfully on Israel's ruin, and they sorrow "a little" (ironic) at the imposition of the Assyrian king.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**Gill** understands "gather them" as gathering the Assyrians against Israel for destruction, or gathering the Israelites into Samaria to be cooped up and taken captive.

*Source: Gill (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)*

**NET Bible note:** The Hebrew verb for "gather" (*qavats*) is often used positively for regathering a dispersed people, but here it is used negatively — "to assemble (people) for judgment" (cf. Ezek 20:34; Hos 9:6).

*Source: NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

**Guzik** sees a note of mercy: "God promised that Israel would face the conquering Assyrians and exile, but also that He would one day gather them again. This note of mercy is sprinkled through the song warning of judgment."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**"Begin to diminish under the oppression of the king of princes":** "King of princes" refers to the Assyrian monarch, whose subordinate rulers were themselves called kings (Isa 10:8). The burden of Assyrian taxation and oppression would gradually wear Israel down.

---

## v. 11 — "Though Ephraim multiplied the altars for sin, they became his altars for sinning."

**Multiplication of altars:** Contrary to the law (Deut 12:5ff), which required a single central sanctuary to preserve the unity of worship and the nation. The narrative in Joshua 22 shows that unity of altar was considered essential to national unity. Israel built many altars — ostensibly for sin offerings — but these became altars where they actually *sinned* by mixing Yahweh-worship with Baal-worship.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**Guzik:** "Israel foolishly built many altars for sin. So it is no surprise that those altars became altars for sinning. When we give ourselves opportunity and occasion for sin, it is never surprising when we end up sinning."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

---

## v. 12 — "Though I wrote for them the great things of My law, they regarded them as something strange."

**God as the author of Scripture:** This is a key text for the divine inspiration of the Bible. God says "I wrote for him the great things of My law." Guzik and Spurgeon both emphasize this strongly.

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**Spurgeon's sermon on this verse** (Sermon No. 15, 1855): Spurgeon declares, "This volume is the writing of the living God: each letter was penned with an Almighty finger; each word in it dropped from the everlasting lips; each sentence was dictated by the Holy Spirit." He says, "There is nothing in this Bible which is unimportant. Every verse in it has a solemn meaning." He laments that "there is dust enough on some of your Bibles to write 'damnation' with your fingers."

*Source: Enduring Word, quoting Spurgeon (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**"Great things" (or "ten thousand precepts" / "a multitude of My precepts"):** Ellicott notes the imperfect tense "I write" represents the continuous process — prophetic teaching as well as the ancient Mosaic law. The Hebrew conveys abundance: God lavishly provided instruction, but Israel treated it all as foreign or irrelevant.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**"Regarded as something strange":** In their idolatry, God's word seemed foreign, alien, irrelevant. Guzik connects this to 1 Cor 2:14 — "the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**NET Bible:** "I spelled out my law for him in great detail, but they regard it as something totally unknown to them!"

*Source: NET Bible (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)*

---

## v. 13 — "Though they offer sacrifices … the LORD does not accept them … They will return to Egypt."

**Outward ceremony without inward devotion:** Israel continued to bring the prescribed sacrifices and eat the fellowship meals, but God rejected the whole thing because their hearts remained in idolatry and rebellion. The sacrifices were mere flesh-eating; God "has no pleasure in them."

*Sources: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**"Return to Egypt":** Ellicott says this means either a literal return to Egyptian bondage or, more likely, the disastrous hankering after Egyptian alliances that would prove futile. Egypt here represents a reversal of the Exodus — going back to the house of bondage they were delivered from, undoing salvation history.

*Source: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)*

**Guzik:** "Sure, they still brought sacrifices to the LORD. But it was all just an outward ceremony because they were still steeped in sin and idolatry. Therefore, their sin remained uncovered, and God will remember their iniquity and punish their sins."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

---

## v. 14 — "Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces; Judah has multiplied its fortified cities…"

**Two nations, two sins, one judgment:**

- **Israel** forgot God and "built temples" (or palaces/temple-palaces — the same Hebrew word used sixty times for Jehovah's temple). Ellicott says "the building of these temple-palaces was a distinct sin against the unity of the Godhead." Instead of worshipping the Creator, they built rival shrines.

- **Judah** multiplied fortified cities, trusting in military defenses rather than in God. This was a subtler sin than Israel's outright idolatry, but equally culpable. Sennacherib's inscription from 701 BC boasts of capturing "forty-six of his (Hezekiah's) strong cities, fortresses" — these were built by Uzziah and Jotham (2 Chron 26:10; 27:4). Their walls would not protect them; only the LORD preserved Judah from total destruction (Isa 37:33–36).

*Sources: Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**Guzik:** "Perhaps we can capture some of the ungodly heart of Israel and Judah by examining our own attraction to grandness and nice facilities. … They can easily become idols if our hearts turn away from God."

*Source: Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)*

**G. Campbell Morgan** (cited by Precept Austin): "Whenever a nation forsakes God it ensures its ruin. It may, for a time, dwell in luxury, building palaces; and give itself a sense of security, by fortifying its cities; but sooner or later the Divine fire will destroy the cities, and devour the castles."

*Source: Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary)*

---

## Notes on Traditions and Differing Views

### Baptist View
- **Gill** (older Baptist, 18th century): Reads the chapter as a catalog of Israel's sins with corresponding punishments. Emphasizes the hypocrisy of Israel's profession, the folly of self-appointed kings, and the logic that a craftsman-made idol cannot be God. Sees the "gathering" of v. 10 as God's judgment, not restoration. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/8.htm)

- **Spurgeon** (Baptist/Reformed): Made Hosea 8:12 the text for a famous sermon on the Bible's divine authorship. He emphasized that God is the author, that Scripture contains only "great things," and that the natural man treats it as "a strange thing." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/ via quotation; original sermon at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/hosea-8.html — not fully retrieved)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: On v. 9, notes Israel is compared to "a stubborn, obstinate ass, controlled by folly, undisciplined, heady, untamable." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/hosea-8.html)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic View
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word)**: Emphasizes practical application — altars for sin become altars for sinning (we create our own stumbling blocks); God's Word seems strange when our hearts are far from God; outward ceremony cannot cover inward rebellion; even good things like church buildings can become idols. While warning of judgment, he notes God's mercy: "Now I will gather them" in v. 10 is a promise of eventual regathering. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-8/)

### Anglican (Older)
- **Ellicott** (1878): Provides careful philological and historical notes. He emphasizes the irony in Hosea's language, the scorn of God toward the calf ("loathsome"), and the debated interpretation of v. 10. He reads "return to Egypt" as either literal return or disastrous hankering after Egyptian alliances. Notes that the "temples" of v. 14 were a sin against the unity of the Godhead. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/hosea-8.html)

### Evangelical (Non-Denominational)
- **Precept Austin**: Draws on a wide range of evangelical sources. Provides extensive word studies (ʿābar, pasha), covenant theology framing (the Mosaic covenant as marriage covenant), and the fulfillment of Deut 28:49. Notes that even the severe warning of the trumpet is an expression of God's mercy — giving Israel one final opportunity to repent. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-8-commentary)

### Modern Scholarship
- **NET Bible notes**: The eagle/vulture is possibly the griffon vulture. The phrase "that they might be cut off" (v. 4) is ironic — they made idols for prosperity, but the result was destruction. The "gathering" of v. 10 uses *qavats* in a negative sense — assembling for judgment, not restoration. (https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Hos&chapter=8)
